coherence.reasons: Both run the same clean chain: market, unit economics, customers, cash, alternative, each ending in a 'do not launch, fund software' governing thought that the slide titles support. X's executive summary is tight and every title maps to a summary line. Y adds an explicit frame on slide 3: six conditions the founders' hypothesis needs, each tied to a section and a verdict, so the hierarchy from governing thought to evidence is more visibly tested. Y also links the Zipcart analysis to a re-entry trigger (about 1,050 orders a day), while X's four conditions sit more loosely on the earlier analysis. Y has one internal inconsistency: the slide 7 sensitivity chart labels are out of order against the values, though the text conclusion is correct. Y's 'loses money on every order' also sits slightly awkwardly with its own Zipcart-city slide. Net, Y is marginally more structured.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred recommendation (R1) with re-entry conditions. Y weighs alternatives better. It models a one-store pilot explicitly and rejects it because even median density loses $6.17 and the runway floor is breached in month 10, which is the key's R4 trap. It also tells the board not to extend the pop-up. X only compares the launch with software and a 'reopen later' option. Y stress-tests its own recommendation: software holds the runway rule only if ARR growth stays at 34% or more, so hires are phased against signed contracts with a 90-day checkpoint. X asserts that runway 'stays well above 12 months' at 60% growth with no downside case. Y's re-entry triggers are more specific and operational (AOV of $42 or more, 3.0 orders per rider-hour, about 1,050 orders a day, or a fee losing under 15% of volume, plus ring-fenced funding). X's 'rider pay rules are settled' is a weaker condition. Y also weighs the first-mover risk and the conflict of competing with grocer customers; X notes the latter too.

evidence.reasons: Both get the core numbers right: −$6.17, −$1.76, −$12.57, about −$1.05 to −$1.10 with Zipcart's moves, $2.5M and about 6 months of runway, −$18.2M for nine stores, and $11M software break-even ARR. X's figures all check out, including the $63.4 break-even AOV, the 27.6-month payback and the stepwise plan gains summing to +$2.02; I found no numerical errors. X is also more careful in wording ('average order') and notes that 'nobody owns the Midwest' cannot be tested. Y uses the critical evidence more fully. It gives the CAGR of 41.5%, break-even AOV at best-observed inputs (about $50), and the break-even density under Zipcart's fee (about 1,042 orders a day), which engages the key's K9 that a profitable route exists only at high density. It also adds a one-driver-at-median sensitivity, a rider-pay sensitivity (+$1.48 per order) and a scale sanity check ($266M of sales against QuickBasket's $210M). Against that, Y's slide 7 chart mislabels three of the sensitivity bars (the text is right), 'every order' is a slight overstatement, and it relies on more self-built model assumptions, though these are flagged in an appendix. Y's deeper use of the decisive evidence outweighs the labelling slip, but only narrowly given X's cleanliness.

revision.reasons: Both reject the founders' hypothesis, as the key expects, and both grant the part that is true (market growth is real). Y handles it more explicitly and fairly. It states the hypothesis, breaks it into six conditions that would have to hold, tests each and concludes 'fails on every condition, so we reverse it'. It tests the founders' capability-edge claim directly against the pop-up, which ran below median on all four drivers. It gives the 'fair caveat' that the pop-up was early, then shows ramp-up alone still leaves −$6.17. On the Zipcart evidence it concedes that 'a profitable route may exist, but only at top-quartile density with premium pricing', which matches the key's nuanced reading. X also deals with Zipcart and computes −$1.1 at the median, but frames it mainly as a rebuttal ('pricing that cost volume, not better operations') and does not quantify what density would make it work. X's handling of the hypothesis is implicit rather than structured.

overall.reasons: Both documents are strong, numerically accurate and reach the defensible conclusion with re-entry conditions. X is leaner and has no errors. Y would serve the board better because it anticipates the likely compromise (a one-city pilot) and shows why it fails. It also shows both readings of the $9.5M with a monthly cash path, and stress-tests the recommended software path down to a 34% growth floor with phased hires and a 90-day checkpoint. It engages the Zipcart counter-evidence to the point of naming the density at which re-entry would make sense, and turns that into measurable triggers. Y's chart-label slip and heavier modelling assumptions are minor against that extra decision value.
